record.original_question: Is the gravitational mass inferred from orbital motions equal to the integral of a source's energy density, for macroscopic sources such as the Sun or for microscopic sources? The problem is to establish whether the energy-density moment used in Einstein gravity is observationally justified, rather than merely sufficient in weak-binding regimes where the exterior Newtonian potential can scale with the number of constituent sources.

evidence.quote: While these two densities are of course proportional in the weak binding limit, we note that in general in order to recover Newton’s original result that the gravitational potential be an extensive function of the amount of matter in the gravitating source, we only need establish proportionality to the number density, and not necessarily to the energy density, a point on which we will capitalize below when we study the fourth order theory.

While the expressing of the Newtonian coefficient as a fourth moment rather than a second moment integral of the energy-momentum tensor is unfamiliar, we should note that it violates no known observational information, since it is only required to hold within fundamental microscopic sources (or within macroscopic compact sources for which nothing at all is currently observationally known).

However, despite its commonplace familiarity, we are not aware that such integrals have ever been performed for either microscopic or macroscopic sources for that matter, and it is simply not known whether the mass of the Sun as determined by the gravitational motions of the planets is in fact equal to the integral of its energy density, since the energy density function of the Sun is unknown).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In Einstein's general theory of relativity, the active gravitational mass of a stationary, weakly self-gravitating source is identified, via the linearized field equations, with the volume integral

M = ∫ T^{00}(x) d^3x

of the time-time component of the stress-energy tensor (i.e., the energy density) over the source. This identification underlies the Newtonian limit in which the exterior potential is Φ(r) = −GM/r.

Establish whether this identification is observationally justified in either of the following two regimes, or exhibit a model-independent argument or measurement that does so:

(1) Macroscopic sources (e.g., the Sun): Show that the gravitational mass M_grav inferred from the orbital (Keplerian/post-Newtonian) motions of test bodies in the exterior field is in fact equal to ∫ ρ_E(x) d^3x, where ρ_E is the internal energy density of the source. Equivalently, rule out alternative source functionals (such as integrals of the number density of constituents, or higher moments of T^{μν}) that would reproduce the same exterior weak-field potential Φ(r) = −GM_grav/r without being equal to ∫ ρ_E.

(2) Microscopic sources: Show that for fundamental microscopic constituents the gravitational mass that enters the exterior Newtonian potential equals ∫ T^{00} over the constituent, as opposed to merely being proportional to the number of constituents or to some other moment of the internal energy-momentum distribution.

In each case, determine whether current observational information can distinguish ∫ T^{00} from alternative source moments, given that in the weak-binding limit the exterior potential is required only to scale extensively with the amount of matter in the source.
artifact.category_tag: Foundations of gravitation / source of Newtonian potential
artifact.status_search_result: Standard astronomical practice determines GM (the gravitational parameter) of the Sun and planets to very high precision from orbital motions, but the search did not surface any observational or theoretical work that directly verifies the equality between the gravitationally inferred mass and the volume integral of the internal energy density for the Sun or for microscopic sources. The interior energy-density profile of the Sun is not directly observed, and no independent measurement appears to have established that ∫T^{00} (rather than another moment of the stress-energy tensor or a count of constituents) is the correct source functional. The status is therefore best classified as unknown / unresolved by observation.

status_evidence.title: Standard gravitational parameter - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The standard gravitational parameter GM of celestial bodies is determined from orbital observations to much higher accuracy than G or M individually.
status_evidence.claim: Orbital observations fix GM but do not independently measure the internal energy-density integral of the source.

status_evidence.title: Changes in the Sun's mass and gravitational constant estimated using modern observations of planets and spacecraft
status_evidence.snippet: Hundreds of thousands of positional observations of planets and spacecraft are used to estimate the Sun's gravitational parameter under post-Newtonian approximations.
status_evidence.claim: Observational mass determinations of the Sun rely on its exterior gravitational field, not on probing its interior energy-density distribution.

status_evidence.title: Solar mass - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The Sun's mass is determined from its gravitational effect on orbiting bodies via Kepler's third law.
status_evidence.claim: No direct observational test verifies that the gravitating mass equals the volume integral of the Sun's energy density.
